> Sometimes people who don't actually understand the law make spurious claims that those investors are legally required as fiduciaries to put their funds into the highest yielding investments. But in reality there is no such requirement

The requirement is what a lawyer can convince a dozen jurors the requirement should be. If there's a lawsuit against a fund manager at an institutional investor saying "you didn't fulfill your duty as a fiduciary because x", there's at least some risk that x becomes a real responsibility for fiduciaries through the outcome of that case. If the zeitgeist dictates that as a responsibility, it is a responsibility.

> They can underweight Meta stock if they believe it's overvalued due to potential legal risks or corporate governance problems or whatever.

The fact that they aren't doing so when the company is losing billions of dollars in legal judgments would suggest either

1) They can't do so because they would lose money doing so

or

2) Our system is in need of reform so that when executives direct a company in such a way that it is routinely facing legal exposure, shareholders remove those executives so that corporations act as better citizens and things are handled at the shareholder meeting level instead of the court system level.

comment_text.value:
I think there’s a lot of value in a “stack skill” like this offers. I don’t personally buy that the scaffolding around “markdown source of truth” makes sense; I prefer to work as close to the agent harness as possible. An iterative conversation and then “cool, write a doc to memorialize and then build this” usually goes well for me, keeping the back-and-forth in context for as long as possible.

Since most of the comments are just throwing shade, here’s what this is actually doing:

https://rustoffrails.org/docs#the-stack-in-one-breath

>>>

Axum on hyper (the binary is the web server: HTTP/1.1 + HTTP/2, no app server or nginx needed)

Tokio · SeaORM (SQLite locally,

Postgres in production, same code)

Tailwind

a frontend mode chosen at birth:

htmx (default): Askama (compile-time checked templates) + htmx. No Node. Optional React or Svelte islands.

inertia: React or Svelte pages with Rails-style server routing, via a generated Inertia adapter. The default when you want a JS UI.

spa: a Vite SPA (React Router or SvelteKit in SPA mode) + a JSON API.

api: no UI, for mobile backends and public APIs (in progress).

story_title.value: Rust off Rails: The opinionated web stack for the AI era

Nope; the compiler was supposed to end coding; when the word coding referred to taking an abstract program written on paper and translating it to machine code.

Compilers were first called automatic coders.

The word compiling referred to something more like linking: producing an image containing multiple library routines. In other words, similar to compiling an anthology of works into a book.

After compilers, the word coding to changed to writing program code in any language.

Because the tooling for automatic coding also compiled the bits of code into a larger image, the term compiler/compiling came to be used for the coding part also.

While the terms reshuffled, the concrete reality was simply that people worked less in assembly language, not that fewer people worked or that programming ended.

It depends. In Ontario (or at least Toronto where I live), the fire department and ambulance services are separate. The paramedics are chronically underfunded and the result is that the fire department is constantly running up milage on multiple expensive and massive fire trucks for routine calls that should just have been a paramedic. This also compounds traffic issues when they park at their destination.

It makes sense for them to automatically show up for some situations (eg car accidents), but there should be a properly funded triage system.

Same goes for the police, which are often called for situations where there should be some other social workers available (again, there are exceptions where police should also be present in those situations).

comment_text.value:
Well, I honestly believe it is rank incompetence. Speaking as someone who's monthly electronic GST filings, commercial authentications, and digital payments, i.e. continued livelihood, is beholden to cert and PKI authorities like eMudhra having their shit together...

As for the odds of this being state-sponsored... It depends on the state's incentive, weighed against its continued behaviour, over the last 10-odd years. Everything below is easy to substantiate with citations. There are too many to cite... I put myself at real risk just by stating any of the following under my real name.

  ---My take: Never attribute to malice, what one can to (rank) incompetence.---
I expect eMudhra-esque collossal gaffes, as a normal course of life, stemming from the apathetic, insular, feudal-minded, shoddily run bureaucracies that the majority of our government and quasi-government organisations are.

Basic day-to-day operations being unavailable, because "Sorry sir, site is down." is a normal everyday life experience of their own staff, not to mention the common person. eMudhra is one of that tribe, and I'd say they are not the worst offenders of the lot, by a wide margin. I'd probably give the "best of the worst" title to our national Employee Provident Fund.

Of course, one can't totally rule out nation-state-level stupidity, such as BGP poisoning by the Pakistanis.

  ---Nation-state action: Wither sufficient incentive? ---
If our current federal administration has incentive to do it, they will... And, given their track record, if it does turn out to be nation-state-engineered for short term tactical gains (to hell with the consequences for anyone else), all I will do is sigh and move on with my day. Cornered politicians can go to any length to save their own skin (usually, just to save face)... Collateral damage be damned. Popular examples include world superpowers bombing distant nations, for whatever gain or goal (usually short-term, because well you most probably won't be President a second time (and never a third)), using whatever pretext they can sell to get others to also get behind (the individual's psychological cover in a firing squad, scaled up to many allied powers).

In India, absolute majority governments have amply demonstrated the same failure mode as US heads of state empowered with de-facto fatwa powers, as of the US PATRIOT act. Given motive and incentive, they easily turn the full might of their uncheckable wrath and ire at our constitution, as well as directly at the common public.

You know, like sending out military forces to "calm down" the pesky student protesters acting against "the national interest".

As we speak, massive nationwide student protests have been bringing shame and angst to the government of our ruling party at the centre (BJP and allies), as well as their various governments across states. Many protests have happened at this scale in the last decade+ of the same ruling party's unbroken streak as a majority power in the centre (federal government). Those other protests were like water off a duck's back. The ongoing student protests, for reasons I've not dug into, appear to be a clear and present existential threat to the incumbents.

My gut feeling is... the incumbents aren't passing the electoral vibe check any more.

The sentiment on the streets of the national capital, and large urban centres nationwide---almost entirely comprised of a new crop of young voters (18 y.o. up to early 30s)----is that they feel robbed of an economically viable future. They've organised at scale (millions on the street) with persistence (they are literally owning the "Cockroach" epithet thrown at them by the powers that be). And in short order, material consequence---unprecedented in its decade-long winning streak so far---befell the incumbent party's administration. The Education Minister had to resign, and they've generally lost face with that whole voting-age cohort. Brand-name loss of key leadership is further disrupting their internal party cohesion. Plenty of hopefuls in there, salivating after the top dog position, but thus far too weak to sway the cult following of the public faces of the party. Even an hint of weakness gives the wannabes a real opening to try. Textbook demagoguery.

If that is indeed true, then in their place, I too would seriously worry about losing even more ground in the next national election... It's not far now. Because? "Winning by overwhelming majority" has been the one and only priority of the incumbents, driving all their work post-election (where work includes constitutional shenanigans)... Being a populist party borne of, and cultivated by far-right nationalist ideologues (the RSS and "Sangh" community), with a longstanding desire for religious supremacy (Hindutva and Sanatan dharma), they publicly and loudly dream of a hundred-year golden age. Uh, no, now I think it's become a thousand-year era (really!). That's not totally insane if you're suddenly goated at winning electoral politics, because our head of state can enjoy unlimited tenure. Yes, you heard that right, India has no constitutional limits to number of re-elections to the Big Chair, whether successive or alternating.

Without looking at absolute numbers, I feel confident that the influx of new voters (lots of people can turn 18 in a single government tenure) far outstrips the older ("whatsapp uncle / aunty") voter base that the incumbents pander to. This has been a lucky break for the fumbling Congress party because their legacy name is finally regaining some cachet... The much-mocked Rahul Gandhi presents like someone the young'uns can actually talk to, like a human being.

But the Gandhi-brand Congress were once an absolute majority power too. At which time they suspended our constitution, and weaponised federal agencies, and created the playbooks that all future governments have been able to deploy at various scales. I expect nothing less from any other party that grabs absolute majority. Currently it's the BJP. Tomorrow, it could be anybody else. Thus far, it's been the secular-presenting Congress, followed by the Hindutva-majoritarian BJP. Woe betide us if next the Communist Party of India gets a bite at that juicy apple. 'cause, like, I don't have to explain what that sort of government can do with absolute power. <shudders>

  ---Nation-state action: Whither evidence of having the means and using them with impunity?---
Ref: our liberally interpretable Information Technology Act. Among other things, it enables and empowers arbitrary blanket Internet Shutdowns and Blackouts, by local states as well as national authorities, to "protect the peace". In some deeply conflicted areas, like Jammu and Kashmir, censorship measures under martial law would give both, the Great Firewall of China and the Stasi a run for their money.

Ref: at-scale weaponisation of Pegasus, as of 2021. Federal and even state authorities like police departments have weaponised nation-state electronic warfare technology with impunity. Usual suspects / targets are politically inconvenient individuals and groups... opposition politicians, bureaucrats with a spine or conscience, students, media, artists, NGOs etc...

All this mixes badly with pre-existing supercharged Sedition laws. These effectively obviate habeus corpus, and are routinely used to prosecute speech interpreted as anti-national / seditious under the generous ambit of our IT laws (we don't have a real privacy law). Mere suspicion and/or fear and/or dislike + Pegasus + garbage IT laws = authority can brazenly plant incriminating evidence on your device... it's reportedly been done multiple times.

People have been held in prison for less (just inconvenient speech), without possibility of bail, for months and years on end, without trial. The main goal is to cause irreparable reputational damage, to create future deterrence... It's pretty effective. A secondary goal is to take the stubborn ones off the board, with no legal recourse, until they break. And of course, to permanently defang the truly outspoken and indomitable few... Some of those people have been in high-security federal prison for years on end now.

In conclusion:

I'm confident all federal administrations of India, current and future, will hold the lawful means to act wilfully, crudely, with impunity, at scale against India's own citizenry.

I'm not sure whether they currently have enough incentive to have used the eMudhra cudgel, to disrupt the protestors. Sure they could MITM the protestor websites, but it's so much easier to block them and takedown their socials. And for more specific work, they already have field deployments of Pegasus and other MITM / spyware technologies.

It could have been much worse if, say, I routinely drove people around or did any kind of safety-critical work.

Regardless: benzos are not "lightweight" drugs, and giving them to people with any kind of history of substance abuse disorders is a Bad Idea.

In practice that would create even more ineffective veto points that already result in stasis and dysfunction in the US Congress.

For more than a decade the US has been stuck operating by renewing the same budget more or less with minor modifications at random intervals of time depending on the political mood. It always gets approved eventually after occasional pointless, wasteful shutdowns. But nothing actually changes from those veto points, just more routine dysfunction and grandstanding.

Self expiring legislation would very likely end up the same way. Just another pro forma procedural roadblock that wastes time and makes the legislature even less effective at real problem solving instead of posturing.

comment_text.value:
This is basically correct but there is some nuance. First of all, people working on unoriginal or very small scope stuff, such as app clones or ad hoc analyses in notebooks, will never hit that wall. They'll never even know the wall is there. This is a bit annoying, because they then generalize their experience with toy projects and come away with the mistaken belief that anyone could make anything if only given enough tokens. This is most problematic when they are in leadership positions.

However, the real value is in complex, non-trivial, and above all novel code. This has been true for a long time, and it's just as true in open source as it is in industry or academia. Here, agents are far less useful. In fact, the only people I've seen have any kind of success using agents on these kinds of "serious" projects are people who are already serious programmers. They already know how to design and test stuff, they already know how to supervise junior developers, they already have an intuition for which aspects of the project the can safely delegate to a less experienced developer. So they're able to use agents as a "better autocomplete" in their own code, or use it to flesh out the non-essential and more routine aspects of the project, or even just delegate the agents to the role of code reviewer.

Here's the thing though. The less experienced ones, the people who don't already have those skills, they do get burned when they "stick the fork in the socket," as you put it, or in other words when they try to use agents to take on projects they don't fully understand... but they don't learn anything! The ones I've seen, anyway. Relying on agents insulates you from the code, which also prevents you from building a mental model of what's going on under the hood, which in turn makes it impossible to learn anything at all. They just keep yelling at the agents, telling them to fix stuff even though each fix introduces yet another regression in an endless loop... they don't know how to dig themselves out of the hole they've dug. And after all, what is the solution? To spend five years down in the code mines, paying your dues as a junior dev, reading and typing and thinking about mere code for the requisite 10,000 hours? Nobody has the time or inclination for that.

Agents, in other words, break the learning loop. You can't learn to program, and therefore can't learn to design or architect software, not really, if you're using agents. I am unfortunately coming to the sad conclusion that the last programmer has already been born; if you didn't have 5+ years of experience and a pretty good handle on the more advanced aspects of programming (such as software architecture, design patterns, optimization, debugging, etc.) before agentic programming became a thing, then I don't see how you ever will.

It'll be like COBOL programmers - the industry will shrink from the top-down, with the first to go being the new college graduates looking to enter the workforce. Inexperienced devs have always been given less interesting projects, but they stuck it out because they were learning valuable skills, building experience, making the economically rational decision to invest in their own career. But anyone entering the market today will never get out of that trench - anyone that actually needs a real programmer for a serious project will hire someone with decades of experience - there will be plenty of supply. And the projects on offer for junior devs won't teach them how to program, only to supervise agents. As a knock-on effect, smart young people already see the writing on the wall and are pivoting to other majors, which just reinforces the trend. This might cause problems in a few decades when all the real programmers start to retire, but when has the market ever considered long term consequences?

comment_text.value:
If you take a step back here, there has always been a group of people who have "shipped code to production" — in the sense of being responsible for the software that was produced -- without ever reading it or knowing it in detail. I am talking about your engineering management. Maybe not your line manager but certainly your director.

I think a useful perspective is "How does engineering management control software quality?" You will know the answers to this question: testing practices, design documents, SLAs, release management. You will know this because you almost certainly have to comply with some of these as a SWE. All of those practices exist because code produced by humans is not perfectly reliable and thus there need to be checks and risk reduction steps to manage the software that is shipped.

The way I view agents is that all of us have become engineering managers now. So those tools are now your tools. You set up the practices and frameworks and make the agents use them. If you set them up right you can be very confident in what the agents wrote without ever reading it.

Now you're not going to go from nothing to "Hey I ship code I've never read" overnight. It takes work. You have to set up your project carefully so that the agents can’t make mistakes. But all you have to do is be systematic about it. Every time the agents do something stupid or they ship a bug, you think, "How do I put something in place to prevent this entire class of bugs from happening again?" As you iterate this process, you will continuously be ruling out entire classes of bugs and eventually you'll be able to trust the agents.

Example: I had a bug, or a class of bugs, where agents would write a database migration and it would be wrong. It would get rolled out and the database would be broken. I fixed this by putting in a migration testing framework where there was data written in an old schema, then the migrations would run on that data. Then you could write tests on the expected result at any point after any migrations. Then, I put in place a rule: if you write a database migration you have to write a migration test. That fixed the problem. I have never had a migration failure since.

So this is not some magical process. It's going to take you hard work to set up your system with all of this infrastructure to make the agents maximally productive. But as you iteratively improve your system, you can reach a place where you can have agents ship code without reading it. It's not just about making the system work but it's also about building your trust in the system that you have. I routinely ship code without reading it now and I think I've shipped about two bugs in the past two months (and I’ve written ~500k LOC in that time). And one of those bugs was very explicitly my fault for telling the agents they could violate one of the frameworks in place (oops).

comment_text.value:
But you never heard someone say "you should still code in assembly so you can understand what your compiler is doing".

Would I routinely code in assembly today? Not for (almost) any new project.

Can I understand assembly and have I used that skill to understand performance problems or debug unexpected behaviour (including some that really did turn out to be caused by bugs in popular compilers)? Absolutely.

I'm not generally a fan of the comparison between what LLMs do and what compilers do. Compilers might vary in their output for given source code but they still follow (hopefully) well-defined specifications. Their behaviour is deterministic and the behaviour of their output is deterministic. With sufficient understanding you can reason about that output or diagnose faults in the compiler behaviour if you ever need to. None of this is true for LLMs.

comment_text.value:
Thanks :)

Still working on some of the data-parallel recognition in LLVM IR space. In order to support both C and C++ with the same data-parallel section extraction, I moved the detection from the ‘xc source code’ phase to the IR lowering phase, meaning that everything could ‘feed in’ to the same routines. That’s caused a little friction with the slightly different ways the LLVM IR from clang and xc’s IR encode loops. The above results are all single-loop extractions and the double-loop ones are still ongoing.

The system works in 3 stages: 1) by being greedy about which loops could possibly vectorise and marking them, 2) by analysing the IR to reject loops which do pointer-aliasing, or object manipulation, or… and then 3) by measuring the fastest way these known-safe kernels could execute.

Which brings me onto one nice thing I haven’t mentioned: that the GPU choice(s) are made at runtime, not compile time, and the system automatically measures (and then persists so it doesn’t have to measure again) the fastest way to run a kernel on the current machine. It handles MSL on Apple devices, PTX on Nvidia cards, Spir-v on Windows, Linux, and Android, and WGSL in the browser. It’ll quite happily divide up the parallel task across a 3090 and a 5080 on my Windows test box for example, with the 5080 doing ~2/3 of the work, because the scheduler is opportunistic.

All without writing anything other than plain C with nary a mention of the GPU. Give me a week or two, and I’ll probably announce it on phoronix (which might then get a mention on HN if it goes down well there, and it’ll be a different url so hopefully won’t be insta-dead).

I'd prefer 8086 segmentation any day over the headache of trying to execute 6502 code from a bank-switched cartridge with a single banking window and a write-only banking register.

comment_text.value:
The VCS has some handy features that makes it easier.

First, there is no frame buffer (there could be no such thing in that memory space), but there are effectively line buffers for the different sprite types and background. These are not in the 128 bytes of general purpose RAM but memory mapped to the display controller.

Second, it maintains the patterns in these buffers until you change them and will repeat them on the next line unless you do anything to change them. This makes it easy to perform partial update, e.g. only update the background every 8 lines and only update sprite graphics on odd lines or whatever you need to do to save time.

Third, the video controller can be instructed (via a memory mapped register) to halt the CPU until the next horizontal "blanking" interval. This makes synchronizing to the beam position between lines much easier.

Fourth, there are no interrupts (except NMI, only triggered manually with the brk instruction) so timing is easily predictable.

Fifth, there is a hardware timer which makes it easier to keep track of your budget while in the vertical blanking portion of the screen, where you probably want to handle most if not all of your game logic. That way the game logic doesn't need to be strictly timed in the same way the screen is.

I made a game for it (https://text.garden/jupitersumo.html) expecting it to be difficult, but found that the simplicity and predictable timing made it surprisingly easy. On the C64 for example you will often find yourself wanting to synchronize to the beginning of a line or even every line for one reason or another, but doing that while dealing with the complexities of its timing is a whole science unto itself. For the main game screen I ended up using some 16 bytes of state in RAM to represent the stuff I need to keep track of while "racing the beam". The code that handles the display is maybe 150 instructions long and lives in the game ROM. The source code is linked from the page if you're interested in how it works.

Of course, in terms of what it displays, my game is very simple, only showing a background and the player sprites. There are much more complex display routines ("kernels") in the VCS game library. An interesting example is Pitfall II, which is very impressive considering the platform, but uses a coprocessor on the cartridge itself (called the DPC) to help sequence line register updates. From memory, I think it lets you enqueue data in advance, and during the display routine the CPU can just read a single register to get the next byte from a queue.

Sebastian Raschka has a good introductory piece on what Looped Transformers usually refer to in practice: https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/gpt-6-astra-looped-t...

One of the big points is that looped architectures don't necessarily remove CoT style reasoning. They definitely change it, but the model can still be prompted for this kind of output. It just spends more computation on individual tokens. I think the hope, in that particular scenario, is that the model spends less tokens on things like backtracking.

But there are lots of approaches to looped transformer architectures. Some have some kind dynamic loop (i.e. they might loop until they satisfy some kind of equilibrium, or they might have some kind of routing function that makes different tokens loop differently, or any number of other approaches). Others are simpler "loop this many times" architectures. It's a really active area of research with some pretty deep roots, if you want to dig in! This paper blew up a while ago, and it's a looped transformer architecture (though not like the ones discussed here) that isn't autoregressive, as an example: https://arxiv.org/html/2510.04871v1

Hi HN. STROT compiles a decision task — "route these tickets", "score this feedback", "classify this text" — into a standalone pipeline. A large LLM is used once, at compile time, to synthesize the labels, the input projection, and the handlers. At runtime a small local model (144M, CPU) makes every decision: ~60ms/record, $0 marginal, zero LLM calls, bounded typed-JSON output.

The goal was to move the expensive, nondeterministic part (an LLM) entirely to build time and keep runtime frozen, cheap, local, and auditable — the way a compiler moves work off the hot path.

What I think is actually interesting, beyond "small model does inference":

- The compiler measures instead of guessing. It scores candidate labelings on a teacher-labeled sample and keeps the winner; on the identical model that's +18pp on a routing benchmark (92.5% vs 74.8%) and +14pp on text classification (86.7% vs 72.7%) over naive integration. - It fits a conformal-calibration threshold at compile time, so low-confidence records abstain with a marginal error guarantee rather than guessing. - A golden-record gate rejects any compile that fails known-answer examples — synthesis is stochastic, and I show that variance in the benchmarks.

What it doesn't do: it can't make a small model understand things it fundamentally can't. On tweet hate-speech it hits the model's ceiling; the fix there is a task-trained model in the swappable slot, not the compiler. All of it — including the losses — is in the repo's benchmarks with reproducible scripts.

There's a browser demo (a 144M model ( which is changeable ) playing Pac-Man, one decision per frame) and a quickstart that runs in a few lines. MIT licensed, pure-stdlib core.

Happy to go deep on the calibration math, the compile/cache design, or where this does and doesn't make sense.

Routing requests to compliant infrastructure covers where the model runs. With ITAR there is still the question of who inside the company gets to see the answer. Export rules apply to foreign persons, including employees working in the US (the deemed export case). So if an agent can pull controlled technical data through a tool call or a retrieval step, a non-US-person engineer who asks the right question gets it back, whichever endpoint served the request.

Do you pass user attributes like US-person status or program access through the gateway, so retrieval and tool calls can be filtered per request? Or is that expected to live in each customer's own systems?

I work at Permit, which builds authorization tooling, so this is the part I always end up asking about.

comment_text.value:
I think you are right, and I should have done a search on that before. Found now that FBP inventor cites someone Weinberg from 1975 about them (though FBP is supposed to be from around 69-70, so might be a somewhat parallel discovery):

> Now what are "IN" and "OUT" that our pseudocode receives IPs from and sends them to? They are not the names of connections, as this would tie a component's code to one place in the network, but are things called "ports". "Portae" means "gates" in Latin, and ports (like seaports) can be thought of as specific places in a wall or boundary where things or people go in or out. Weinberg (1975) describes a port as

"... a special place on the boundary through which input and output flow... Only within the location of the port can the dangerous processes of input and output take place, and by so localizing these processes, special mechanisms may be brought to bear on the special problems of input and output."

https://www.jpaulmorrison.com/fbp/concepts_book.shtml

Still, I'm amazed at how it took so long before they became mainstream in data flow oriented libraries and DSLs.

And it seems J.P. Morrison was also highlighting Named ports as particularly useful, which is also perhaps what I should have highlighted in my initial comment above.

It's gotten better lately it seems, but a lot of tools skipped that part, which now requires tons of specialized syntax just for routing of multiple parallel streams.

---

Thank you for kind words!

comment_text.value:
It seems "solved" to me, and I've been designing circuits and PCBs for 40 years.

I recently asked Claude (Opus 5.5) to design a wifi fan speed controller based on the ESP32 microcontroller. I told it to design a circuit for KiCad 10. I told it to write the software based on the ESP-IDF framework (for ESP32). I told it I would design the PCB based on the schematic it created.

It went to work. About 15 or 20 minutes later, it was done.

Everything looked good. Parts selection was reasonable. The first schematic was kind of weird, every part was placed on its own without any interconnected lines, so I had it re-do the schematic to show the part interconnections. It did a pretty good job.

Then I went to work designing the PCB. I had to find a project case and gave Claude some JPG images from the amazon page of the case dimensions, and it created a perfect PCB outline complete with mounting holes for the PCB.

I designed the PCB, but it's been a while since I did anything with mains voltage (120v here in the US). I asked Claude to analyze my PCB design, and it pointed out some issues with my trace routing, like not putting low-voltage traces crossing high-voltage traces, etc.

I then directed Claude to design its own PCB based on the project case constraints, and it did a fantastic job - way better than I did, honestly. It separated all the high voltage areas of the circuit from the low voltage areas, and clearly marked them with warnings on the silk screen.

I had it do all the part selection, and I purchased the parts - I'm not giving it my credit card to order parts, I can still do something useful towards this project.

I did not have to install anything for Claude to do any of this, it installed whatever tool it needed, and it generated the KiCad files.

So, this seems like PCB design is "solved".

Claude also wrote all the software for the ESP32 in another folder, including a web-based interface to control fan speed.

The PCBs and parts are on their way to me now. I guess I'll find out in about a week how "solved" this really is, but looking at the PCB design, it's looking really good.

Now it probably helps that I have 40 years experience doing exactly these tasks, so I can tell when something is going to work or not, and I know how to tell Claude what I want. Someone new to circuit/PCB design might have a more difficult time because you don't know what you don't know. I was very specific about the kind of circuit and parts I wanted - an ESP32 controlling a Triac controlling mains voltage with an optocoupler, etc - this is something I've built myself decades ago, so I already knew what "solved" looks like.

story_title.value: AI-assisted PCB design for KiCad 10

The sound card took sound computation off the CPU as well. Back in the day, every aspect of the game was fighting for CPU cycles.

Way back in the day there were some very impressive (given the technology) arcade ports to things like the Apple ][. That system's audio required running an assembly function that literally touched a memory address over and over again at a specific time rate; each touch flipped the electromagnet on the speaker. So games with theme music had to time slice hanging out in the audio routine versus doing anything else.

I grew up with a copy of Moon Patrol on Apple ][c and I didn't know for years that the theme song isn't supposed to sound like it's being played through a tea kettle.

I will give this a try! I feel like AI should be able to automate this process (Schematic and/or PCB). I made a new design 2 months ago; tried to get Claude and COdex to do the schematic in KiCad, and they were not effective. Made a mess of it for an initial build, and edits later. I didn't bother with the component placement and routing.

I did find LLMs to be very effective on answering questions about routing, part selection, and identifying problems; was using a new MCU (Atmosic) with some unusual power circuitry, and got a working board first go. LLMs also crushed getting it working with rust (Very likely I am the first person to program an Atmosic MCU in rust); found a debugger that would work (NXP MCU-Link; the St-Linkv3s I normally use won't work for this, and the official recommended part is very expensive). The LLMs wrote a probe-RS configuration for it, linking scripts etc.

The LLMs also, under close direction, wrote a minimal HAL subset for I2C, SPI, power management, clocks, and BLE. I pointed it to my STM32 HAL as an API guide, set up the basic data structures, and pointed it to the Atmosic SDK (In C). It connected the dots, and produced a working HAL with a familiar API.
